"**November Rain**" is a song by American [hard rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock "Hard rock") band [Guns N' Roses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guns_N'_Roses "Guns N' Roses"). Written by the band's lead vocalist [Axl Rose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axl_Rose "Axl Rose"), the [power ballad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_ballad "Power ballad") was released in February 1992, by [Geffen Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geffen_Records "Geffen Records"), as the third single from the band's third studio album, *[Use Your Illusion I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Use_Your_Illusion_I "Use Your Illusion I")* (1991). The song peaked at number one on the US [*Cash Box* Top 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cash_Box_Top_100_Pop_Singles "Cash Box Top 100 Pop Singles") and number three on the [*Billboard* Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100"), and at almost nine minutes long it was the longest song to enter the top ten of the chart at the time of its release. As of 2019[\[update\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=November_Rain&action=edit), it was the fourth longest song to enter the Hot 100 chart.[\[3\]](#cite_note-3) Additionally, "November Rain" reached number two on the [Portuguese Singles Chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_Singles_Chart "Portuguese Singles Chart"), number four on the [UK Singles Chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UK_Singles_Chart "UK Singles Chart"), and the top 10 on several other music charts around the world. The accompanying music video was directed by [Andy Morahan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Morahan "Andy Morahan").

## Background

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=November_Rain&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")\]

[Slash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slash_\(musician\) "Slash (musician)") states in his autobiography that the band recorded in 1986 an 18-minute version of "November Rain" at a session with guitarist [Manny Charlton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manny_Charlton "Manny Charlton") (of rock band [Nazareth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazareth_\(band\) "Nazareth (band)")) the year prior to beginning sessions for *[Appetite for Destruction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appetite_for_Destruction "Appetite for Destruction")*.[\[4\]](#cite_note-Bozza-4): 151 

According to a story [Axl Rose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axl_Rose "Axl Rose") reported during the 2006 leg of the [Chinese Democracy Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Democracy_Tour "Chinese Democracy Tour"), no other band members wanted to participate in the production of this song (or the other notable ballad "[Estranged](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estranged_\(song\) "Estranged (song)")"). Slash and [Duff McKagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duff_McKagan "Duff McKagan") were opposed to the band's drift to symphonic ballads, feeling their choice of more direct rock songs were being overlooked by Rose. Eventually, Rose persuaded the others during work at Can-Am Studios (where some of the album was recorded and mixed). Slash disputed Axl's claims of harsh musical differences in his autobiography released the next year.[\[4\]](#cite_note-Bozza-4): 454 

Slash reported that his guitar solo in the song's album version developed directly from an improvisation.[\[4\]](#cite_note-Bozza-4): 316 [\[5\]](#cite_note-5)

## Writing and composition

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=November_Rain&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Writing and composition")\]

"November Rain" is the third-longest song by Guns N' Roses, behind "[Coma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coma_\(Guns_N'_Roses_song\) "Coma (Guns N' Roses song)")" (10:14) from the same album, and "[Estranged](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estranged_\(song\) "Estranged (song)")" (9:24) from *[Use Your Illusion II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Use_Your_Illusion_II "Use Your Illusion II")*. It was the longest song ever to reach the top 10 of the [*Billboard* Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100") until November 2021, when surpassed by Taylor Swift's extended rerecording of "[All Too Well](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_Too_Well "All Too Well")".[\[6\]](#cite_note-6)[\[7\]](#cite_note-7)[\[8\]](#cite_note-8) The song's composition was influenced by [Elton John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elton_John "Elton John")'s 1973 opus "[Funeral for a Friend/Love Lies Bleeding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funeral_for_a_Friend/Love_Lies_Bleeding "Funeral for a Friend/Love Lies Bleeding")".[\[9\]](#cite_note-rollingstone-9)

Its distinct symphonic overtone owes to a sweeping string arrangement, orchestrated by Rose.[\[4\]](#cite_note-Bozza-4): 318 [\[10\]](#cite_note-10) "We call it 'the [Layla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Layla "Layla") song'," joked Slash, referencing a similarly constructed rock song with a long, instrumental second part.[\[11\]](#cite_note-11) It was later preceded by the coda from "Layla" on the [Not in This Lifetime... Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Not_in_This_Lifetime..._Tour "Not in This Lifetime... Tour").

On November 4, 2022, the track was re-released with newly recorded orchestration on a re-issue of the *Use Your Illusion* album. A 50-piece orchestra conducted and arranged by [Christopher Lennertz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Lennertz "Christopher Lennertz") played the parts that had been [ sampled audio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sampling_\(music\) "Sampling (music)") in the original mix.[\[12\]](#cite_note-12) The track was mixed by [Steven Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_Wilson "Steven Wilson").[\[13\]](#cite_note-13)[\[14\]](#cite_note-stevenwilson-mix-14)

## Critical reception

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=November_Rain&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Critical reception")\]

[Robert Hilburn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Hilburn "Robert Hilburn") from *[Los Angeles Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Times "Los Angeles Times")* wrote, "This sweeping [ballad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballad "Ballad") – reminiscent of [Elton John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elton_John "Elton John") and [Bernie Taupin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernie_Taupin "Bernie Taupin")’s most majestic work – underscores the ambition and range of the best and most volatile American [hard-rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock "Hard rock") group in a decade."[\[15\]](#cite_note-15) Dave Jennings from *[Melody Maker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melody_Maker "Melody Maker")* said, "There's probably no other band who can match the Gunners' ability to sound frighteningly real and then laughably crass in rapid succession. \[...\] On "November Rain", they fit both extremes into one nine-minute epic ballad."[\[16\]](#cite_note-16) Another editor, Simon Reynolds, declared it as "a lush, swoony, mock-orchestral epic mid-way between [Trevor Horn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trevor_Horn "Trevor Horn"), [Jim Steinman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Steinman "Jim Steinman") and '[Purple Rain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purple_Rain_\(song\) "Purple Rain (song)")'."[\[17\]](#cite_note-17) Parry Gettelman from *[Orlando Sentinel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orlando_Sentinel "Orlando Sentinel")* viewed it as "a schlocky, over-produced ballad".[\[18\]](#cite_note-18) Richard Harrington from *[The Washington Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Washington_Post "The Washington Post")* felt that in the wake of their breakthrough power ballad "[Sweet Child o' Mine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweet_Child_o'_Mine "Sweet Child o' Mine")", Guns N'Roses "have wisely chosen to play to their female constituency" with "November Rain". He explained that the song "finds [Axl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axl_Rose "Axl Rose") in an Elton John mood with a piano, synthesized strings and the realization that while 'It's hard to hold a candle/ in the cold November rain,' we should 'never mind the darkness/ we can still find a way/ cause nothin' lasts forever/ even cold November rain.' On the other hand, at almost nine minutes, this song comes close."[\[19\]](#cite_note-19)

## Chart performance

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=November_Rain&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Chart performance")\]

In the United States, the song peaked at number three for two weeks in 1992, making it Guns N' Roses' sixth and last top-10 hit. It stayed in the top 10 for 10 weeks and on the [Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot_100 "Hot 100") for 30 weeks.[\[20\]](#cite_note-20) The song also peaked at number nine in Germany and remained on the chart for 51 weeks.[\[21\]](#cite_note-ger-21) In Australia, "November Rain" was ranked at number two on the 1992 end-of-year chart despite only reaching number five on the [ARIA Singles Chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ARIA_Singles_Chart "ARIA Singles Chart").[\[22\]](#cite_note-aus-22) It was included on ARIA's year-end charts in two consecutive years (1992 and 1993, when it appeared at 36).[\[23\]](#cite_note-ausye92-23)[\[24\]](#cite_note-ausye93-24) A similar situation took place in New Zealand, where the song peaked at number seven but stayed in the top 20 for 24 non-consecutive weeks, ending 1992 as New Zealand's second-best-selling single.[\[25\]](#cite_note-nz-25)[\[26\]](#cite_note-nzye-26)

## Music video

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=November_Rain&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Music video")\]

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/c/ca/November-rain-dress.jpg/250px-November-rain-dress.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:November-rain-dress.jpg)

Composite image of the wedding dress from the "November Rain" music video worn by [Stephanie Seymour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Seymour "Stephanie Seymour")

The music video for "November Rain", directed by British director [Andy Morahan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Morahan "Andy Morahan"),[\[27\]](#cite_note-27) was inspired by [Del James](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Del_James "Del James")'s short story "[Without You](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Del_James#Without_You "Del James")", for which he is credited in the long version of the video. The short story portrays a rock star struggling to come to terms with the loss of his girlfriend, who died by suicide (gunshot) after he repeatedly strayed from their relationship. *November Rain* is one of the [most expensive music videos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_most_expensive_music_videos "List of most expensive music videos") ever made.[\[28\]](#cite_note-28)

The video tells a story reminiscent of "Without You", and features a live performance footage from Los Angeles' [Orpheum Theater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orpheum_Theatre_\(Los_Angeles\) "Orpheum Theatre (Los Angeles)").[\[29\]](#cite_note-kerrang-29) First, in a silhouette, Rose's character is seen going to bed and taking pills; a bottle of whisky is also visible next to him. The scene, now in color, changes to the wedding of the main characters, played by Rose and his then-girlfriend [Stephanie Seymour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Seymour "Stephanie Seymour"). The other band members are among the many guests.

Slash's character realizes he forgot the wedding rings, when McKagan's character offers his rings as a substitute. After the wedding couple leaves the church, we see the wedding reception that is later interrupted by sudden, heavy rain, causing everyone to run for shelter.

The next scene shows a funeral at the same church. Rose's character grieves at the death of his wife, now inside a casket with a mirrored object obscuring half of her face. A heavy rain falls upon the cemetery when the casket is laid to rest.

A final scene shows Seymour's character back at the wedding, tossing her white bouquet, which turns red in the air and lands on her coffin. Black and white scenes of Rose's character's nightmares show a mix of wedding and funeral scenes. The music video ends with Rose's character kneeling beside her grave and the bouquet turns back to white as the rain washes the red color away.

For the outside shots of Slash's first guitar solo, Rose had originally envisioned it taking place in a "cool field". Because the video was shot in winter, however, there were no good-looking fields around, and the band decided to film in [New Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Mexico "New Mexico"), where they had a church building transported specifically for the shoot.[\[29\]](#cite_note-kerrang-29) The larger church, for the wedding scenes, is Los Angeles' [St. Brendan Catholic Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Brendan_Catholic_Church,_Los_Angeles "St. Brendan Catholic Church, Los Angeles").[\[29\]](#cite_note-kerrang-29)

The music videos for "November Rain", "[Don't Cry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don't_Cry "Don't Cry")" and "[Estranged](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estranged_\(song\) "Estranged (song)")" form an unofficial trilogy of sorts. While never specifically confirmed by the band, Del James' short story "Without You" served as inspiration for the video, and received recognition in the video's end credits.

In July 2018, the music video became the first video created prior to YouTube to surpass one billion views.[\[30\]](#cite_note-30)[\[31\]](#cite_note-31) In February 2023, the music video reached another milestone after it surpassed two billion views and remaining the oldest song (from the early 1990s) to achieve that feat.[\[32\]](#cite_note-32)

The video was re-released in November 2022, with the newly synced orchestration, to promote the *Use Your Illusion (Super Deluxe Edition)* box set.[\[33\]](#cite_note-33)

## Retrospective response

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=November_Rain&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Retrospective response")\]

"November Rain" was voted number one on the [Rock 1000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rock_\(New_Zealand\) "The Rock (New Zealand)") 2006, an annual countdown of the top 1,000 rock songs by New Zealand radio listeners. It was voted number two on the 2007 version, beaten by "[Back in Black](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Back_in_Black_\(song\) "Back in Black (song)")" by [AC/DC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AC/DC "AC/DC").[\[35\]](#cite_note-35) The song topped the "album tracks" section of a 1993 readers' poll in GN'R [fanzine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fanzine "Fanzine") *Controversy*, beating "[Coma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coma_\(Guns_N'_Roses_song\) "Coma (Guns N' Roses song)")". The top ten was completed by "[Estranged](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estranged_\(song\) "Estranged (song)")", "[Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_War_\(song\) "Civil War (song)")", "[Paradise City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paradise_City "Paradise City")", "[Sweet Child o' Mine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweet_Child_o'_Mine "Sweet Child o' Mine")", "[Don't Cry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don't_Cry "Don't Cry")", "[Welcome to the Jungle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welcome_to_the_Jungle "Welcome to the Jungle")", "[Patience](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_\(Guns_N'_Roses_song\) "Patience (Guns N' Roses song)")" and "[Mr. Brownstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mr._Brownstone "Mr. Brownstone")".[\[36\]](#cite_note-36)

The song placed number 140 on [*Pitchfork*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pitchfork_\(website\) "Pitchfork (website)")'s "Top 200 Tracks of the 90s".[\[37\]](#cite_note-37) In Chile, the song placed at number 73 on Chilean radio [Rock & Pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_&_Pop_\(Chilean_radio\) "Rock & Pop (Chilean radio)").[\[38\]](#cite_note-38) In 2017, *[Paste](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paste_\(magazine\) "Paste (magazine)")* ranked the song number nine on their list of the 15 greatest Guns N' Roses songs,[\[39\]](#cite_note-39) and in 2020, *[Kerrang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerrang! "Kerrang!")* ranked the song number six on their list of the 20 greatest Guns N' Roses songs.[\[40\]](#cite_note-40)

[NPR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NPR "NPR") described the song as "one of the ultimate [hard-rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard-rock "Hard-rock") [power ballads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_ballad "Power ballad")",[\[1\]](#cite_note-npr-1) while [VH1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VH1 "VH1") added that the song "is the sprawling, cosmic-reaching, just-so-insane-it-works hard rock epic toward which every previous single-track hard rock epic had led and from which every subsequent single-track hard rock epic has emerged".[\[41\]](#cite_note-41) *Glide Magazine* named the song at second in their list of "Favorite [Hair-Metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glam_metal "Glam metal") Power Ballads".[\[42\]](#cite_note-glide-42)

"**November Rain**" is a song by American [hard rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock "Hard rock") band [Guns N' Roses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guns_N'_Roses "Guns N' Roses"). Written by the band's lead vocalist [Axl Rose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axl_Rose "Axl Rose"), the [power ballad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_ballad "Power ballad") was released in February 1992, by [Geffen Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geffen_Records "Geffen Records"), as the third single from the band's third studio album, *[Use Your Illusion I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Use_Your_Illusion_I "Use Your Illusion I")* (1991). The song peaked at number one on the US [*Cash Box* Top 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cash_Box_Top_100_Pop_Singles "Cash Box Top 100 Pop Singles") and number three on the [*Billboard* Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100"), and at almost nine minutes long it was the longest song to enter the top ten of the chart at the time of its release. As of 2019[\[update\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=November_Rain&action=edit), it was the fourth longest song to enter the Hot 100 chart.[\[3\]](#cite_note-3) Additionally, "November Rain" reached number two on the [Portuguese Singles Chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portuguese_Singles_Chart "Portuguese Singles Chart"), number four on the [UK Singles Chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UK_Singles_Chart "UK Singles Chart"), and the top 10 on several other music charts around the world. The accompanying music video was directed by [Andy Morahan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Morahan "Andy Morahan").

## Background

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=November_Rain&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Background")\]

[Slash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slash_\(musician\) "Slash (musician)") states in his autobiography that the band recorded in 1986 an 18-minute version of "November Rain" at a session with guitarist [Manny Charlton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manny_Charlton "Manny Charlton") (of rock band [Nazareth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazareth_\(band\) "Nazareth (band)")) the year prior to beginning sessions for *[Appetite for Destruction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appetite_for_Destruction "Appetite for Destruction")*.[\[4\]](#cite_note-Bozza-4): 151 

According to a story [Axl Rose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axl_Rose "Axl Rose") reported during the 2006 leg of the [Chinese Democracy Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Democracy_Tour "Chinese Democracy Tour"), no other band members wanted to participate in the production of this song (or the other notable ballad "[Estranged](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estranged_\(song\) "Estranged (song)")"). Slash and [Duff McKagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duff_McKagan "Duff McKagan") were opposed to the band's drift to symphonic ballads, feeling their choice of more direct rock songs were being overlooked by Rose. Eventually, Rose persuaded the others during work at Can-Am Studios (where some of the album was recorded and mixed). Slash disputed Axl's claims of harsh musical differences in his autobiography released the next year.[\[4\]](#cite_note-Bozza-4): 454 

Slash reported that his guitar solo in the song's album version developed directly from an improvisation.[\[4\]](#cite_note-Bozza-4): 316 [\[5\]](#cite_note-5)

## Writing and composition

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=November_Rain&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Writing and composition")\]

"November Rain" is the third-longest song by Guns N' Roses, behind "[Coma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coma_\(Guns_N'_Roses_song\) "Coma (Guns N' Roses song)")" (10:14) from the same album, and "[Estranged](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estranged_\(song\) "Estranged (song)")" (9:24) from *[Use Your Illusion II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Use_Your_Illusion_II "Use Your Illusion II")*. It was the longest song ever to reach the top 10 of the [*Billboard* Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100") until November 2021, when surpassed by Taylor Swift's extended rerecording of "[All Too Well](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_Too_Well "All Too Well")".[\[6\]](#cite_note-6)[\[7\]](#cite_note-7)[\[8\]](#cite_note-8) The song's composition was influenced by [Elton John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elton_John "Elton John")'s 1973 opus "[Funeral for a Friend/Love Lies Bleeding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funeral_for_a_Friend/Love_Lies_Bleeding "Funeral for a Friend/Love Lies Bleeding")".[\[9\]](#cite_note-rollingstone-9)

Its distinct symphonic overtone owes to a sweeping string arrangement, orchestrated by Rose.[\[4\]](#cite_note-Bozza-4): 318 [\[10\]](#cite_note-10) "We call it 'the [Layla](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Layla "Layla") song'," joked Slash, referencing a similarly constructed rock song with a long, instrumental second part.[\[11\]](#cite_note-11) It was later preceded by the coda from "Layla" on the [Not in This Lifetime... Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Not_in_This_Lifetime..._Tour "Not in This Lifetime... Tour").

On November 4, 2022, the track was re-released with newly recorded orchestration on a re-issue of the *Use Your Illusion* album. A 50-piece orchestra conducted and arranged by [Christopher Lennertz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Lennertz "Christopher Lennertz") played the parts that had been [ sampled audio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sampling_\(music\) "Sampling (music)") in the original mix.[\[12\]](#cite_note-12) The track was mixed by [Steven Wilson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_Wilson "Steven Wilson").[\[13\]](#cite_note-13)[\[14\]](#cite_note-stevenwilson-mix-14)

## Critical reception

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=November_Rain&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Critical reception")\]

[Robert Hilburn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Hilburn "Robert Hilburn") from *[Los Angeles Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Times "Los Angeles Times")* wrote, "This sweeping [ballad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballad "Ballad") – reminiscent of [Elton John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elton_John "Elton John") and [Bernie Taupin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernie_Taupin "Bernie Taupin")’s most majestic work – underscores the ambition and range of the best and most volatile American [hard-rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard_rock "Hard rock") group in a decade."[\[15\]](#cite_note-15) Dave Jennings from *[Melody Maker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melody_Maker "Melody Maker")* said, "There's probably no other band who can match the Gunners' ability to sound frighteningly real and then laughably crass in rapid succession. \[...\] On "November Rain", they fit both extremes into one nine-minute epic ballad."[\[16\]](#cite_note-16) Another editor, Simon Reynolds, declared it as "a lush, swoony, mock-orchestral epic mid-way between [Trevor Horn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trevor_Horn "Trevor Horn"), [Jim Steinman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Steinman "Jim Steinman") and '[Purple Rain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purple_Rain_\(song\) "Purple Rain (song)")'."[\[17\]](#cite_note-17) Parry Gettelman from *[Orlando Sentinel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orlando_Sentinel "Orlando Sentinel")* viewed it as "a schlocky, over-produced ballad".[\[18\]](#cite_note-18) Richard Harrington from *[The Washington Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Washington_Post "The Washington Post")* felt that in the wake of their breakthrough power ballad "[Sweet Child o' Mine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweet_Child_o'_Mine "Sweet Child o' Mine")", Guns N'Roses "have wisely chosen to play to their female constituency" with "November Rain". He explained that the song "finds [Axl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axl_Rose "Axl Rose") in an Elton John mood with a piano, synthesized strings and the realization that while 'It's hard to hold a candle/ in the cold November rain,' we should 'never mind the darkness/ we can still find a way/ cause nothin' lasts forever/ even cold November rain.' On the other hand, at almost nine minutes, this song comes close."[\[19\]](#cite_note-19)

## Chart performance

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=November_Rain&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Chart performance")\]

In the United States, the song peaked at number three for two weeks in 1992, making it Guns N' Roses' sixth and last top-10 hit. It stayed in the top 10 for 10 weeks and on the [Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot_100 "Hot 100") for 30 weeks.[\[20\]](#cite_note-20) The song also peaked at number nine in Germany and remained on the chart for 51 weeks.[\[21\]](#cite_note-ger-21) In Australia, "November Rain" was ranked at number two on the 1992 end-of-year chart despite only reaching number five on the [ARIA Singles Chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ARIA_Singles_Chart "ARIA Singles Chart").[\[22\]](#cite_note-aus-22) It was included on ARIA's year-end charts in two consecutive years (1992 and 1993, when it appeared at 36).[\[23\]](#cite_note-ausye92-23)[\[24\]](#cite_note-ausye93-24) A similar situation took place in New Zealand, where the song peaked at number seven but stayed in the top 20 for 24 non-consecutive weeks, ending 1992 as New Zealand's second-best-selling single.[\[25\]](#cite_note-nz-25)[\[26\]](#cite_note-nzye-26)

## Music video

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=November_Rain&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Music video")\]

[![](//thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/c/ca/November-rain-dress.jpg/250px-November-rain-dress.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:November-rain-dress.jpg)

Composite image of the wedding dress from the "November Rain" music video worn by [Stephanie Seymour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Seymour "Stephanie Seymour")

The music video for "November Rain", directed by British director [Andy Morahan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Morahan "Andy Morahan"),[\[27\]](#cite_note-27) was inspired by [Del James](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Del_James "Del James")'s short story "[Without You](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Del_James#Without_You "Del James")", for which he is credited in the long version of the video. The short story portrays a rock star struggling to come to terms with the loss of his girlfriend, who died by suicide (gunshot) after he repeatedly strayed from their relationship. *November Rain* is one of the [most expensive music videos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_most_expensive_music_videos "List of most expensive music videos") ever made.[\[28\]](#cite_note-28)

The video tells a story reminiscent of "Without You", and features a live performance footage from Los Angeles' [Orpheum Theater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orpheum_Theatre_\(Los_Angeles\) "Orpheum Theatre (Los Angeles)").[\[29\]](#cite_note-kerrang-29) First, in a silhouette, Rose's character is seen going to bed and taking pills; a bottle of whisky is also visible next to him. The scene, now in color, changes to the wedding of the main characters, played by Rose and his then-girlfriend [Stephanie Seymour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Seymour "Stephanie Seymour"). The other band members are among the many guests.

Slash's character realizes he forgot the wedding rings, when McKagan's character offers his rings as a substitute. After the wedding couple leaves the church, we see the wedding reception that is later interrupted by sudden, heavy rain, causing everyone to run for shelter.

The next scene shows a funeral at the same church. Rose's character grieves at the death of his wife, now inside a casket with a mirrored object obscuring half of her face. A heavy rain falls upon the cemetery when the casket is laid to rest.

A final scene shows Seymour's character back at the wedding, tossing her white bouquet, which turns red in the air and lands on her coffin. Black and white scenes of Rose's character's nightmares show a mix of wedding and funeral scenes. The music video ends with Rose's character kneeling beside her grave and the bouquet turns back to white as the rain washes the red color away.

For the outside shots of Slash's first guitar solo, Rose had originally envisioned it taking place in a "cool field". Because the video was shot in winter, however, there were no good-looking fields around, and the band decided to film in [New Mexico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Mexico "New Mexico"), where they had a church building transported specifically for the shoot.[\[29\]](#cite_note-kerrang-29) The larger church, for the wedding scenes, is Los Angeles' [St. Brendan Catholic Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Brendan_Catholic_Church,_Los_Angeles "St. Brendan Catholic Church, Los Angeles").[\[29\]](#cite_note-kerrang-29)

The music videos for "November Rain", "[Don't Cry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don't_Cry "Don't Cry")" and "[Estranged](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estranged_\(song\) "Estranged (song)")" form an unofficial trilogy of sorts. While never specifically confirmed by the band, Del James' short story "Without You" served as inspiration for the video, and received recognition in the video's end credits.

In July 2018, the music video became the first video created prior to YouTube to surpass one billion views.[\[30\]](#cite_note-30)[\[31\]](#cite_note-31) In February 2023, the music video reached another milestone after it surpassed two billion views and remaining the oldest song (from the early 1990s) to achieve that feat.[\[32\]](#cite_note-32)

The video was re-released in November 2022, with the newly synced orchestration, to promote the *Use Your Illusion (Super Deluxe Edition)* box set.[\[33\]](#cite_note-33)

## Retrospective response

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=November_Rain&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Retrospective response")\]

"November Rain" was voted number one on the [Rock 1000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Rock_\(New_Zealand\) "The Rock (New Zealand)") 2006, an annual countdown of the top 1,000 rock songs by New Zealand radio listeners. It was voted number two on the 2007 version, beaten by "[Back in Black](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Back_in_Black_\(song\) "Back in Black (song)")" by [AC/DC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AC/DC "AC/DC").[\[35\]](#cite_note-35) The song topped the "album tracks" section of a 1993 readers' poll in GN'R [fanzine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fanzine "Fanzine") *Controversy*, beating "[Coma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coma_\(Guns_N'_Roses_song\) "Coma (Guns N' Roses song)")". The top ten was completed by "[Estranged](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estranged_\(song\) "Estranged (song)")", "[Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_War_\(song\) "Civil War (song)")", "[Paradise City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paradise_City "Paradise City")", "[Sweet Child o' Mine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweet_Child_o'_Mine "Sweet Child o' Mine")", "[Don't Cry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don't_Cry "Don't Cry")", "[Welcome to the Jungle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welcome_to_the_Jungle "Welcome to the Jungle")", "[Patience](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patience_\(Guns_N'_Roses_song\) "Patience (Guns N' Roses song)")" and "[Mr. Brownstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mr._Brownstone "Mr. Brownstone")".[\[36\]](#cite_note-36)

The song placed number 140 on [*Pitchfork*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pitchfork_\(website\) "Pitchfork (website)")'s "Top 200 Tracks of the 90s".[\[37\]](#cite_note-37) In Chile, the song placed at number 73 on Chilean radio [Rock & Pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_&_Pop_\(Chilean_radio\) "Rock & Pop (Chilean radio)").[\[38\]](#cite_note-38) In 2017, *[Paste](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paste_\(magazine\) "Paste (magazine)")* ranked the song number nine on their list of the 15 greatest Guns N' Roses songs,[\[39\]](#cite_note-39) and in 2020, *[Kerrang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerrang! "Kerrang!")* ranked the song number six on their list of the 20 greatest Guns N' Roses songs.[\[40\]](#cite_note-40)

[NPR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NPR "NPR") described the song as "one of the ultimate [hard-rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hard-rock "Hard-rock") [power ballads](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Power_ballad "Power ballad")",[\[1\]](#cite_note-npr-1) while [VH1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VH1 "VH1") added that the song "is the sprawling, cosmic-reaching, just-so-insane-it-works hard rock epic toward which every previous single-track hard rock epic had led and from which every subsequent single-track hard rock epic has emerged".[\[41\]](#cite_note-41) *Glide Magazine* named the song at second in their list of "Favorite [Hair-Metal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glam_metal "Glam metal") Power Ballads".[\[42\]](#cite_note-glide-42)
